research.bullet: Buyers describe cloud agents as dispatch, not autocomplete: the deliverable is a branch and a PR, so statics should show the artifact, not the editor.
research.citation: a branch and a PR, not a suggestion in your editor.
research.section: §2 Buyers & workflows — A. Self-serve / power developers

research.bullet: Engineering leads gate trust on review capacity, not generation volume. Copy should promise something reviewable, never more output.
research.section: §2 Buyers & workflows — B. Engineering / platform leads

research.bullet: The live buyer fork is verifiability: a finished diff to check versus watch-and-interrupt. Task shape, not model quality, picks the tool.
research.citation: Devin hands you a finished diff to check, Claude Code lets you watch and interrupt… I pick by how verifiable the task is.
research.section: §2 Buyers & workflows — B. Engineering / platform leads

research.bullet: Enterprise language is governance-shaped: fleets under permissions, sandboxing, audit trail, bounded autonomy. Modernization claims stay qualitative without public proof.
research.citation: governed fleets; permission controls / isolated sandbox / audit trail / bounded autonomy

research.bullet: The nearest developer-static format peer runs copy-led, one-job workflow cards. Mirror that density and CTA clarity, not their product nouns.

batch_direction: The five statics share warm off-white surfaces, restrained grotesque typography, generous margins, a plain DEVIN wordmark, and one small blue mono tag. The heroes introduce a single abstract line motif each; the volume concepts differentiate through right alignment, an offset black enterprise composition, and a stepped headline. Use the permitted DEVIN wordmark throughout rather than reconstructing a symbol that conflicts with the supplied official lockups.

concepts.name: Assign, walk away, review
concepts.icp: Free → Pro $20 IC developer who owns a ticket queue
concepts.jtbd: I want to hand off a well-scoped ticket and come back to a finished pull request instead of babysitting an editor.
concepts.insight: The async dispatcher frame is already how developers describe cloud agents, so the ad reads as category language rather than a vendor promise.
concepts.proof: The shipped PR: branch, diff, and CI status on a well-scoped ticket, reviewed the next morning

copy.primary:
Assign the ticket. Walk away. Review the PR.
Devin plans, runs the work, and comes back with a branch and a pull request.
You still own the merge.
copy.headline: Assign the ticket. Review the PR.

kill_metric.rationale: This angle is pure hook clarity, so weak click-through means the dispatcher frame is not landing cold.

citation.quote: Assign the ticket. Walk away. Review the PR.

concepts.name: Inspect the receipt
concepts.icp: Pro $20 IC developer, agent-skeptical, reviews everything before merge
concepts.jtbd: Before I merge anything an agent wrote, I need to see the diff, the CI run, and what it actually did.
concepts.insight: Skeptics convert on inspectability, not capability claims, and Desktop is the surface where the session artifacts live.
concepts.proof: Session artifacts: the diff, CI result, and session recording inside Devin Desktop

copy.primary:
Do not trust the demo. Inspect the proof.
Every session leaves a diff, a CI run, and a recording.
Review it like a sharp intern, then merge.
copy.headline: Diff, CI, recording. Then you merge.

kill_metric.threshold: < 8 download starts per 100 LP sessions after 500 LP sessions (7 days)
kill_metric.rationale: The promise is inspectable sessions, so if people read it and will not open the surface that shows them, the proof frame failed.

citation.quote: Diff + CI + recording — then you merge.

concepts.name: Stop rationing the agent
concepts.icp: Max $200 IC developer running long multi-repo work past Pro quota
concepts.jtbd: I keep rationing runs so I do not burn quota mid-migration, and I want a plan that matches how much work I actually delegate.
concepts.insight: Quota burn and opaque metering are the live cost objections for heavy self-serve users, so naming the ladder plainly removes the fear that stalls upgrades.
concepts.proof: The published ladder: Free, Pro $20/mo, Max $200/mo — included quota, then dollars for extra work

copy.primary:
Free to start. Pro $20/mo. Max $200/mo.
Included quota, then dollars for the extra work.
Stop rationing runs halfway through a migration.
copy.headline: Pro $20. Max $200. No rationing.

kill_metric.metric: Signup to paid plan (Pro or Max) conversion
kill_metric.threshold: < 4% of signups upgrade within 14 days, after 300 signups
kill_metric.rationale: A price-led static that cannot move signups onto a paid tier is buying curiosity, not intent.

avoid: invented ACU rates or cost-per-PR figures
pay for work not seats on a self-serve card

concepts.name: Bounded autonomy
concepts.icp: VP Eng owning platform and security-adjacent approval for agent rollout
concepts.jtbd: I cannot let an agent touch production repos until permissions, sandboxing, and an audit trail are in place.
concepts.insight: Enterprise agent buyers read control language before capability language, and bounded autonomy is the only enterprise claim we can make without public outcome proof.
concepts.proof: Control surface: permission gates, isolated sandbox, audit trail, session replay — the agent halts rather than guesses

copy.primary:
Permissions, sandbox, audit trail — then the agent works.
Dangerous commands wait for approval. A missing secret halts the run.
Every session replays.
copy.headline: Permissions, sandbox, audit trail.

kill_metric.metric: Landing-page session to demo-form submit rate
kill_metric.threshold: < 1.0% demo submits after 1,500 LP sessions (14 days)
kill_metric.rationale: Governance copy exists to trigger a sales conversation, so a dead form is the honest signal that the control frame is not a buying trigger here.

citation.quote: Permissions, sandbox, audit trail — then the agent works.

avoid: invented security certifications or compliance badges

concepts.name: One playbook, many repos
concepts.icp: CTO funding multi-repo modernization on workload-priced agents
concepts.jtbd: I need the same migration playbook executed across every repo without buying a seat for each engineer who might run it.
concepts.insight: Leaders treat the backlog as a parallelism problem, so fleet execution priced on workload rather than seats matches how they actually budget the work.
concepts.proof: Fleet backlog execution across repos, priced on workload and ACUs rather than seats

copy.primary:
One playbook. Many repos.
Migrations, flaky tests, dependency bumps, coverage gaps — run as a fleet of agents, not a queue of tickets.
Priced on workload, not seats.
copy.headline: One playbook. Many repos. One fleet.

kill_metric.metric: Sales-accepted rate of demos sourced from this angle
kill_metric.threshold: < 30% of demo submits accepted after 25 submits (21 days)
kill_metric.rationale: Fleet and workload language attracts curiosity from every tier, so acceptance rate is the only honest test that it reaches real enterprise budget owners.

citation.quote: (migrations, flaky tests, dependency bumps, coverage gaps) — one playbook / many repos
citation.section: §2 Buyers & workflows — B. Engineering / platform leads

avoid: named customer outcomes without public proof
competitor claims such as team counts or funding figures as Cognition facts
